requirement: Habeas's bundled agent skills MUST NOT offer a waiver for an uncited first-party Rust function. When a function serves only as an internal implementation detail and no existing requirement explains it, Habeas's bundled agent skills MUST direct agents to propose an explicit project requirement, such as `internal-detail`, obtain the user's agreement, cite it on the function, and run `habeas author --all` for the harness to assess its evidence. That assessment MUST account for whether the cited requirement explains the function's behavior. An internal-detail requirement MUST NOT justify an otherwise unspecified end-user-observable behavior.
rationale:
**Verdict:** The bundled skills implement the requirement as written. No test checks the skill wording, and I judge that absence acceptable. Two caveats are below.

**What the requirement asks of the skills** (`md/requirements/cli.md:88-90`):
- offer no waiver for an uncited function;
- direct agents to propose an explicit project requirement such as `internal-detail`, obtain the user's agreement, cite it, and run `habeas author --all`;
- ensure the harness assessment accounts for whether the cited requirement explains the function's behavior;
- not let `internal-detail` justify otherwise unspecified end-user-observable behavior.

**Implementation in the skills**
- `assets/skills/habeas-bootstrap-requirements/SKILL.md:23`:
  - It says "There is no waiver for an uncited function."
  - It says to propose an explicit requirement "such as `internal-detail`", "get the user's agreement, and cite it".
  - It says "Do not use an internal-detail requirement to justify unspecified end-user-visible behavior."
  - Line 25 then directs the agent to run `habeas author --all`. It describes the harness reviewing whole functions against all declarations, and it forbids hand-written evidence.
- `assets/skills/habeas-requirements/SKILL.md:26`:
  - It repeats the no-waiver rule.
  - It says to propose `internal-detail` "for the user's agreement" and cite it on the function.
  - It forbids using it to justify observable behavior.
  - Line 28 says to run `habeas author --all` for the attestation.
- `assets/skills/habeas-evidence/SKILL.md` (lines 44-47 of the supplied range): "propose an appropriate requirement rather than waiving the function or inventing evidence".

**Assessment accounts for whether the requirement explains the behavior**
- `md/requirements/authoring.md` (function attestation prompt) tells the model to "Explain how you identified the applicable set and how the cited declarations account for the function's behavior".
- `md/reference.md:278` and `:282` state the same expectation.

**Tests and citations**
- No `{test}` or `{impl}` reference to `requirements.cli.internal_detail_guidance` exists anywhere. A ripgrep for `internal_detail_guidance|internal-detail` found only the skill text, `md/reference.md` and the requirement itself.
- The requirement is about the wording of static Markdown assets. A string-matching test would only restate the prose.
- `tests/symposium_hook_smoke.py` (~lines 204-265) does check that the shipped skills are installed and refreshed byte-for-byte. That makes the assets the delivered artifact.
- I accept the absence of a dedicated test as justified by the requirement being static documentation.

**Caveats**
- **Citation:** the lack of any citation to this requirement is a minor traceability weakness, not a functional gap.
- **Agreement step:** the `habeas-evidence` skill does not itself mention user agreement. The other two skills do, and all three are bundled together.

description: Build an initial Habeas requirement set from an existing codebase by tracing its tests and user-visible behavior; use for requirements bootstrapping or coverage audits.

Read the project's existing requirements, documentation, public entry points, implementation, and tests before writing new requirements. Follow behavior through the code rather than relying only on test names or top-level dispatch.
- Every first-party runnable test or test case, including integration tests, doctests, and parameterized cases where present. Record the requirement or example IDs each test checks.

- Every explicit function or method in first-party Rust sources, including trait declarations, test helpers, and internal helpers. Record its file location and the requirement or example IDs it cites. Also inventory relevant public APIs, commands, handlers, UI actions, configuration, outputs, errors, and distinct observable branches. Do not count one tagged entry point as coverage for deeper code.
Exclude generated and third-party code from the inventories. If a candidate looks user-facing but its purpose is unclear, keep it on the gap list until resolved.

Treat requirements inferred from existing code as proposals. Show the user their proposed full IDs and exact text, along with uncertainty about whether observed behavior is intended or a bug. Obtain agreement on the proposals before installing them in the mdBook; prior explicit agreement to the same requirements counts.

Create or reuse the agreed, stable, chapter-qualified `{req}` requirements in the mdBook. State observable obligations with BCP 14 terms. Group tests that check the same behavior under one requirement; several tests MAY share an ID. For tests of internal invariants, write a requirement for the invariant they actually check rather than inventing a user-facing promise. Distinguish intended behavior from a possible bug or incidental implementation detail.

Put at least one `{test}` reference with a full requirement or example name on each test definition or individual case. A parameterized test can carry a reference at its case source or generating declaration when that is the only editable source. Add multiple references when a test checks multiple definitions. Do not use one file-level tag to stand in for unrelated tests.

Add a requirement or example reference in a Rust comment attached to each inventoried function or method or within its body. An example must cite a requirement, so an example reference still traces the function to a requirement. A reference on an enclosing module or `impl` does not cover its functions. There is no waiver for an uncited function. If no behavior-specific requirement explains an internal helper, propose an explicit project requirement such as `internal-detail`, get the user's agreement, and cite it. Do not use an internal-detail requirement to justify unspecified end-user-visible behavior.

Run `habeas author --all` to create requirement and example evidence and each function's attestation in `evidence/rust/<rust_file>.json`. Each assessment has its own model conversation. The harness reviews whole functions against all requirement and example declarations, including ones not already cited, to assess citation completeness. It records delivered source inputs and writes judgments and rationales. The supervising agent must not compose or refresh evidence JSON, determinations, rationales, or snapshots itself, or delegate manual evidence writing to another agent. If authoring configuration or credentials are unavailable, report the blocker instead of substituting hand-written evidence.

Review every end-user-observable result and branch, including errors and input handling, when proposing requirements and adding citations. Verify that the code fulfills each applicable requirement and does not introduce additional observable behavior without an agreed requirement. When requirements interact, cite all of them at meaningful implementation points. For example, a `^C` shortcut needs a requirement that explains why it is accepted. A tag alone does not establish that the behavior matches the requirement. Use the bundled `habeas-requirements` and `habeas-evidence` guidance for directive syntax and the authoring workflow.

The harness assesses whether cited implementations meet requirements and whether tests cover interesting cases, allowing a rationale for absent tests when logic is simple or testing is impractical. For examples, it checks the scenario, test setup, and expected assertions; a true judgment needs a covered `{test}` reference. Its outcomes are true for supported subjects, false for unacknowledged gaps or insufficient information, and `{"FIXME": ["#125"]}` for gaps explicitly acknowledged in source comments or tests. A FIXME does not excuse additional unacknowledged gaps. Function-attestation determinations remain boolean judgments of citation completeness.
For example, source comments can carry these references:

After authoring, run the project tests and Habeas validation. Address reported gaps by fixing source, tests, citations, or agreed requirement text, then rerun `habeas author --all` and the tests. Validation checks evidence without invoking models. Have both inventories independently reviewed against the source and tests before claiming complete coverage. Report test-tag coverage and function coverage as mapped counts over total counts. Claim 100% only when both inventories have no unmapped items and every observable branch has been reviewed. List remaining gaps with file locations and reasons; do not invent evidence or silently exclude difficult cases.

description: Design and vet requirements and examples for user-visible behavior changes in a Habeas mdBook project before coding; maintain definitions and references.

When a user requests new or changed user-visible behavior in a Habeas project, first read the relevant requirements, code, and tests. Identify requirements that already express the intended behavior. For gaps, draft the smallest set of observable obligations, including important outcomes and failure cases, without committing to an implementation.

Run `habeas info <glob>` to read current requirement and named example texts, evidence states, rationales, inputs, and validation findings as Markdown. A full name selects exactly; `*` matches any number of characters, including dots, when you need to inspect a group.

Show the user the full IDs and text of existing requirements to reuse, plus the proposed chapter location, full IDs, and exact fenced text of any additions or changes. State open product choices separately. Ask the user to agree to or revise this requirement set. User-provided exact requirement text or explicit agreement earlier in the conversation counts as approval; a general request to build the feature does not. Keep drafts out of the mdBook while review is pending, and do not write implementation or test code yet.

After agreement, install the approved requirements in the mdBook and confirm their names. Then implement the behavior and add tests and traceability references. Run `habeas author --all` to create or refresh evidence and function attestations through the configured model. The supervising agent must not compose evidence JSON, rationales, determinations, or source snapshots itself or delegate manual evidence writing to another agent. If implementation reveals a substantive change to an approved obligation, review and install the revised requirement before coding that change. Missing or false evidence is expected while implementation is incomplete.

The authoring harness assesses whether a requirement's cited code implements it as stated and whether tests cover interesting design cases. For absent tests, it assesses whether simplicity or impracticality justifies their absence. For an example, it assesses whether test setup and assertions cover the scenario and expected outcomes. Use these criteria while implementing and fixing reported gaps; leave evidence judgments and rationales to the harness.

Requirement and example judgments have three outcomes: `true`, `false`, or `{"FIXME": ["#125"]}`. The harness uses FIXME when source comments or tests explicitly acknowledge the uncovered aspects, recording their issue references or other identifying content. A documented gap does not excuse other, unacknowledged gaps. Use the `habeas-evidence` skill for the authoring workflow.

Inspect every end-user-observable result and branch, including errors and input handling. Check that the code fulfills each applicable requirement and introduces no additional observable behavior without an agreed requirement. When requirements interact, cite every applicable requirement at the relevant implementation point and explain how their texts jointly account for the behavior. A citation alone does not explain why a behavior, such as accepting `^C`, is specified.

Every explicit function or method in first-party Rust sources needs its own requirement or example reference in an attached Rust comment or within its body, including trait methods and test helpers. Each example cites a requirement. A reference on an enclosing module or `impl` does not cover its functions, and there is no uncited-function waiver. Do not use an internal-detail requirement to justify otherwise unspecified observable behavior.

It judges whether the function carries **all applicable citations** and records the reviewed inputs. Fix missing citations in source, then rerun the harness; do not create attestations or change their determinations by hand.
Function-attestation determinations remain boolean and judge citation completeness, not whether the requirements are satisfied.

An item with a declared name is declared on the line containing that name; an item without one is declared on the line containing its distinctive keyword or introducer, such as `use` or `impl`. Each input MUST store the repository-relative `rust_file`, the item's syntactic `rust_item` selector, and its complete raw source lines. The command MUST report every selected item and reject a line on which no item is declared.

`habeas add-input --requirements <glob>` MUST add or refresh one requirements input containing the matched full names and their concatenated raw declaration sources. It MUST report the matched names in expansion order and reject a glob that matches no requirement or named example.

Each definition MUST declare exactly one nonempty `:phrase:` option before its explanatory body. The phrase MUST be interpreted as plain text. Definitions MUST NOT require their own evidence records or determinations.

The `{term}` role followed by a backtick-delimited full definition name MUST reference a named definition. In rendered Markdown, the reference MUST display the definition's phrase as an ordinary hyperlink to its anchored declaration, without a badge. The phrase MUST be escaped appropriately for rendering.

Missing targets and targets of another kind MUST be reported. Escaped references and references in Markdown code examples MUST remain literal. A term reference MUST NOT satisfy a requirement citation or a Rust function's requirement-coverage obligation.

Evidence inputs MAY have a definition form containing exactly `definition` and `text`. `definition` MUST identify one named definition; `text` MUST contain its complete raw fenced declaration as source lines, including its phrase option and explanatory body.

Validation MUST reject missing definitions and changed snapshot text, identifying the definition and showing a compact diff when available. Moving an unchanged definition within its chapter MUST NOT invalidate its snapshot. Evidence displays MUST show the definition name, current source location, and recorded text.

Requirement and example evidence MUST include a definition input for every term referenced by its subject text or reviewed inputs. Rust function attestations MUST include definition inputs for every term referenced by their reviewed inputs, including selected requirements and examples.

Habeas MUST repeatedly include definitions referenced by required definitions until the set reaches a fixed point. Each required definition MUST have exactly one definition input per evidence record. Cyclic references MUST be permitted and MUST NOT cause repeated expansion or nontermination.
Validation MUST report missing required definition inputs and MUST NOT silently refresh snapshots.

For every `{impl}`, `{cite}`, and `{test}` reference in a project source file, the evidence file for the referenced requirement or example MUST contain an input whose resolved source ranges cover the reference's file and line. Habeas MUST report every uncovered reference with its role, full name, source file, and line number.

During repository validation, Habeas MUST parse every first-party Rust source file in the project. Every explicitly declared function or method, including trait methods and test helpers, MUST have a valid `{impl}`, `{cite}`, or `{test}` reference to a defined requirement or named example in a Rust comment attached to its declaration or within its body. A named example MUST cite a requirement. A reference in a string literal, on an enclosing module or impl block, or only in an evidence input MUST NOT count. Habeas MUST report every uncited function with its file, line, and name, and MUST report a Rust parse failure instead of silently skipping the file.

A definition glob MUST match a complete full name. `*` MUST match zero or more characters, including dots; all other valid name characters MUST match literally. An empty glob MUST be invalid. The same glob matching rule MUST be used by requirements evidence inputs and CLI definition filters. All three MUST match against both requirements and named examples.

Habeas MUST identify a Rust item by the pair of its repository-relative `rust_file` and a `rust_item` selector derived from a `syn` parse of that file. The selector MUST describe syntactic ancestry within the file and MUST NOT resolve Rust modules across files or use line numbers as identity. Named items MUST use kind-and-name segments such as `fn[run]` and `struct[Packet]`. Impl segments MUST distinguish inherent from trait impls using their syntactic self type and optional trait path. Otherwise identical selectors MUST have deterministic source-order disambiguators. A `use` declaration MUST have a positional selector `use#N`, where N is its one-based position among sibling `use` declarations; its import target MUST NOT form part of the selector. Other items without a suitable name MUST have a kind and positional disambiguator. Selector spelling MUST be documented and reversible when names or types contain delimiter characters.

For every function or method covered by `references.rust_function_coverage`, repository validation MUST require exactly one attestation in `evidence/rust/<rust_file>.json`. Each such file MUST be an object with exactly `rust_file` and `functions`, where `rust_file` matches its repository-relative source path and `functions` is an array. Each attestation MUST contain exactly `rust_item`, `citations`, `determination`, `rationale`, and `inputs`. Its `determination` MUST remain a boolean assessing citation coverage; the FIXME outcome applies to requirement and example judgments. Its `citations` MUST be the nonempty set of valid references owned by the function, each recorded by role and full requirement or example name. Its `inputs` MUST include one Rust-item input selecting the function and at least one requirements input; together, the requirements inputs MUST match every name in `citations`. Habeas MUST validate every input and fail for a missing, duplicate, orphaned, stale, or false attestation, a changed citation set, or an empty rationale. Each finding MUST identify the source file, current line when available, and item selector.

In Markdown, escaped roles and role-looking text in inline code, fenced code, or raw HTML MUST remain literal and MUST NOT count as references. A `{req}` directive inside a fenced code example and a legacy inline `{req}` role MUST NOT define a requirement.

Given a requirement `foo.a.bar` and a named example `foo.a.b.bar`, `foo.*.bar` matches both, in that order. A requirements input stores both full names and their complete raw fenced declarations. Adding another matching definition invalidates the existing input. {cite}`requirements.references.definition_globs` {cite}`requirements.ci.requirements_inputs`

A function attestation has a Rust-item input selecting its function and a requirements input matching the definitions reviewed for it. Changing the function's raw lines or adding a definition matched by the requirements glob invalidates the attestation until the agent reviews it again. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_function_attestations`

Put at least one `{test}` reference with a full requirement or example name on each test definition or individual case. A parameterized test can carry a reference at its case source or generating declaration when that is the only editable source. Add multiple references when a test checks multiple definitions. Do not use one file-level tag to stand in for unrelated tests.

Add a requirement or example reference in a Rust comment attached to each inventoried function or method or within its body. An example must cite a requirement, so an example reference still traces the function to a requirement. A reference on an enclosing module or `impl` does not cover its functions. There is no waiver for an uncited function. If no behavior-specific requirement explains an internal helper, propose an explicit project requirement such as `internal-detail`, get the user's agreement, and cite it. Do not use an internal-detail requirement to justify unspecified end-user-visible behavior.

Run `habeas author --all` to create requirement and example evidence and each function's attestation in `evidence/rust/<rust_file>.json`. Each assessment has its own model conversation. The harness reviews whole functions against all requirement and example declarations, including ones not already cited, to assess citation completeness. It records delivered source inputs and writes judgments and rationales. The supervising agent must not compose or refresh evidence JSON, determinations, rationales, or snapshots itself, or delegate manual evidence writing to another agent. If authoring configuration or credentials are unavailable, report the blocker instead of substituting hand-written evidence.

Inspect every end-user-observable result and branch, including errors and input handling. Check that the code fulfills each applicable requirement and introduces no additional observable behavior without an agreed requirement. When requirements interact, cite every applicable requirement at the relevant implementation point and explain how their texts jointly account for the behavior. A citation alone does not explain why a behavior, such as accepting `^C`, is specified.

If no existing requirement explains an internal helper, propose a project requirement such as `internal-detail` for the user's agreement and cite it on the function. Do not use an internal-detail requirement to justify otherwise unspecified observable behavior.

Fix missing citations in source, then rerun the harness; do not create attestations or change their determinations by hand.

Rust-item selectors use syntactic ancestry within one repository-relative file. Examples include `mod[local]/fn[run]`, `impl[Thing]/fn[run]`, `impl[Thing/Trait]/fn[run]`, `trait[Trait]/fn[read]`, `fn[outer]/fn[inner]`, and positional `use#1`. Duplicate sibling names gain `#1`, `#2`, and so on. Delimiter characters and whitespace within names or impl types use percent-encoded UTF-8 bytes, so spelling can be recovered without resolving modules across files. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_item_selectors`
